events.excerpt: Fused filament fabrication (FFF, also known as FDM) 3Drinting specialist InfiMech has opened crowdfunding for an eight-toolhead 3D printer family, the MX Series — promising "near-zero waste" multi-color and multi-material printing. "Unlike traditional single-nozzle systems that purge material during every single color swap, the InfiMech MX Series utilizes a smart independent tool architecture," InifiMech's Xingshuai Xiong explains of the new printer family. "Each tool purges only once upon its first activation to ensure the melt zone is perfectly filled. Subsequent color switches require no further filament waste throughout the entire print. Printing an eight-color model produces only eight small purge drops in total — reducing material waste and printing time to the absolute minimum." Multi-toolhead printers, contrasted with automatic material switchers, aren't a new concept — but at the cheaper end of the market you're usually limited to four toolheads in total. The InfiMech MX, by contrast, comes with six as standard while the MX Pro moves to eight. The more expensive model, roughly twice the price of the base version, also increasing the printable area from 220×220×220mm to 300×300×300mm, adds a full enclosure, heated print chamber, side-blowing cooling fan, camera, built-in
events.headline: The InfiMech MX and MX Pro Bring Eight Toolheads to Bear on Low-Cost Multi-Material Printing

events.excerpt: It’s hard to believe how lucrative this crime can be: According to a press release from the United States attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, three men ­ Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit ­ were arrested for using AI to alter and impersonate the voices and images of executives and attorneys at various companies in order to convince employees to send over large payments. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain over the summer, while Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. The alleged fraud took place between 2024 and 2026. With the help of AI, the men allegedly acted as a corporate executive, targeting employees of various companies and telling them they needed their help with sensitive financial transactions. They would then instruct the employees to get in touch with lawyers at a large international law firm. The men would then impersonate a lawyer at these firms and have the employees wire a large amount of money. The men ultimately stole more than $129m from companies all over the world including in the US, according to the DoJ. Always remember that there are three parts of AI security: security of AI, security with AI, and security from AI. This is the third.
events.headline: Three People Arrested for AI-Enhanced Impersonation Fraud

Worse yet, I might have had to become a marketer, or a designer, or a human resources specialist…or even a salesperson. Not very long ago (in 2024, and for fifty years before that), software engineers like me were the best robots anyone had access to. The CIO at Disney would ask me to redesign FastPass from the ground up, and I would do it in one long-running process over a weekend while he sipped coffee and watched the game. The head of Dell’s Identity Management business would bring me a huge project, and I would dive in, writing thousands of lines of code by hand. events.excerpt: The following is an opinion post reflecting my vision for a possible design direction for Ethereum, not a concrete design. What I argue for is to rethink the notions of scaling, availability, and finality according to the principles of elasticity. TL;DR Ethereum’s capacity is configured in advance: one block per slot, a fixed slot time, a gas limit and a size limit. Price matches demand to it, and safety margins cover for the network. No protocol-wide rule adapts capacity limits to measured resource pressure. Elasticity is first of all about robustness. An elastic system measures what it can carry and takes on less when it is falling behind. A system without that feedback is the kind that goes into congestion collapse, and Ethereum’s overload incidents look like it. Scaling comes with it. A system that can back off can afford to run close to what the network and the nodes can carry, where a fixed margin has to pay for the worst day every day. TCP is the working example: its congestion control was built to stop collapses, and it is also much of why the same protocol, with small changes, runs on modems and on fibre. I look at the mempool and the unfinalized available chain as two grey areas of work in flight. The second one, its size and what it would cost to lose, is the control s
events.headline: Elastic Ethereum

events.excerpt: "Train in Python, serve in C++" might as well be Google's motto when it comes to much of its ML work. Python is easy for data scientists to wield, but keeping its interpreter in the serving pipeline can add overhead and deployment headaches. The industry-backed OpenXLA Project provides tools for compiling machine learning computations into native code for different processors. The latest component of this setup to be open sourced is XSE , short for the XLA Serving Engine. One-shot inference XSE is not so much suited for large-scale LLM inference (which would be better served by vLLM or SGLang ), but rather for smaller, more sharply task-oriented models, of which there are plenty at Google. "LLM serving gets most of the attention right now, but a significant amount of production inference is still ranking, recommendation, embedding, and vision models. These tend to be short requests with very high [queries-per-second] and tight latency budgets," Nathan Beach , Google director of product management, wrote in a LinkedIn missive Tuesday. At Google, XSE already handles more than six million queries per second across services including YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, and Search. These models aren't there for a leisurely chat. They rank results, recommend videos, and make other decisions on
events.headline: Google gooses Python AI performance by... removing Python

events.excerpt: Hi all, If you work with more than one Cosmos chain, you’ve probably hit this: chain binaries don’t update themselves. After a network upgrade, the gaiad or osmosisd on your machine quietly goes stale, and you find out when a transaction fails or a query returns something odd. Cosmovisor solves this for running nodes, but nothing did for developers, CLI users and CI. I built cosmup to fill that gap. It’s a small Go CLI that reads the Cosmos chain registry, downloads the right binary for your platform, verifies its SHA256, and keeps versions side by side. $ cosmup check osmosis Local: v30.0.0 (/usr/local/bin/osmosisd) Network: v31.0.0 (via https://lcd.osmosis.zone) Status: does not match the network; run: cosmup install osmosis@v31.0.0 $ cosmup install osmosis Verified sha256 d435408b... Active: osmosis v31.0.0 What it does: install / use / list: install any version listed in the chain registry, switch between installed versions instantly check: compares your local binary with the version the live network runs, and shows scheduled upgrades (exits 1 on mismatch, so it works in CI) update: moves every installed chain to its recommended version cosmovisor: for validators, puts a verified upgrade binary into cosmovisor’s upgrades folder ahead of the upgrade height remove / prune: clea
events.headline: Cosmup: install, switch and check Cosmos chain binaries (like nvm, for gaiad/osmosisd/...)

events.excerpt: Summary Reth v2.11.0 is a hardening and performance release. RPC calls that can do unbounded work are now capped or cancellable ( eth_callMany , trace_callMany , debug_traceCallMany , eth_getProof , mev_simBundle , eth_simulateV1 ), and the release brings a broad set of transaction pool, P2P and storage correctness fixes. EIP-7702 authorization recovery is parallelized, P2P skips decoding responses it never asked for, and overlay provider setup is cheaper. SDK users: Ethereum block execution now runs on evm2::block , and reth's executor types are thin adapters over it (see Breaking Changes). Action Required Removed no-op CLI flags. The node now refuses to start if you still pass --engine.legacy-state-root , --engine.caching-and-prewarming , --engine.parallel-sparse-trie , --engine.disable-parallel-sparse-trie , --engine.precompile-cache or --rpc-cache.max-headers (alias --rpc-cache.max-envs ). Drop them from your config ( #28369 ) With --instance N and no explicit --auth-ipc.path , the Engine API IPC socket is now /tmp/reth_engine_api.ipc-N . Set --auth-ipc.path if your consensus client expects the old path ( #28257 ) Explicit IPC socket permissions are now validated at startup, and an invalid mode is a startup error. events.excerpt: UK travelers had more than fog to contend with this week, as Linux proved that if Windows could bork anything, it could bork it better. Spotted by Andy Hinks at Heathrow Airport's Terminal 2, this information display has seen better days. While its neighbors offer walking times and terminal maps, it presents a sideways Linux boot log – useful only if your next connection involves mounting a filesystem. There aren't many clues to what has befallen the machine behind the screen. The boot messages mention systemd , an Intel PRO/1000 network adapter, and an EXT4 filesystem on what appears to be a logical volume named LV_ROOT . Whether mounting that filesystem is the problem, or simply the last thing displayed before something else went wrong, isn't clear. Heathrow's information displays clearly accommodate a mixture of technologies. Recent examples ran Microsoft Windows, which had - naturally - suffered a moment of its own. Linux can evidently be just as unreliable in the right hands. The question is which Linux distribution is having its moment in the sun. Heathrow has been rolling out Raspberry Pi-based signage, although the Intel PRO/1000 adapter leaves the hardware behind this particular display something of a mystery. Pi hardware makes sense for signage: it's relatively cheap –
events.headline: Linux joins Heathrow's grounded fleet of information screens

Our goal is to travel across all 81 provinces, introduce people to Zcash, and help create local connections that can continue after we leave. events.excerpt: The UK government talks a good game about buying British, but less than £1 in every £6 spent with its biggest technology suppliers goes to British firms, according to research exposing how much Whitehall relies on foreign tech. A report from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) found that while 42.5 percent of spending with the public sector's 150 largest technology suppliers appears to go to UK companies, that figure collapses to just 15.4 percent once you look beyond where those businesses happen to be headquartered. A UK headquarters doesn't necessarily make a company British. Some are owned from overseas, others have most of their staff abroad, and many simply resell technology from US giants such as Microsoft. In fact, 43 percent of the spending attributed to UK-headquartered suppliers goes to resellers. Bytes and Softcat alone account for around £2 billion, making them two of the three biggest recipients of public sector technology spending. Once researchers traced reseller contracts back to the companies behind the products, the US emerged as the biggest beneficiary, accounting for £9.2 billion of the £19.2 billion spent with the largest suppliers. events.excerpt: When a module limits what governance can do with it, a cap on what a treasury pays out per week or a list of addresses a reserve is allowed to pay, the easy place for that limit is the module’s params. The authority for MsgUpdateParams is then the same gov account the limit is meant to hold back. That came up in the Luggom thread here in October, and the fix was in their repo the same day. I think it’s general enough for its own topic, because it’s easy to miss when you read the module on its own. What x/gov does when a proposal passes In SDK v0.53.8, the version Gaia v29 runs, the gov EndBlocker tallies the vote and, if it passed, opens one cached context and runs the proposal’s messages in the order they were submitted ( abci.go L166-L217 ). Every message sees what the ones before it wrote. If one fails, nothing is written and the proposal is marked failed. So a proposal with a MsgUpdateParams that adds a payee or raises the cap, followed by the spend, passes the module’s check in the same block. Nothing runs before the vote either. At submission SubmitProposal runs each message’s ValidateBasic , checks that its only signer is the gov account and that the router knows the type ( proposal.go L46-L69 ), and that’s it.
